front_blocks.md: Define **conductor**.

back_blocks.md: A **conductor** is a material that allows **charge** (usually electrons) to flow through it easily. Conductors tend to be **metals**.

front_blocks.md: Define **insulator**.

back_blocks.md: An **insulator** is a material that has **no free charges**, so does not allow the flow of charge through it very easily.

front_blocks.md: Name four examples of **conductors**.

back_blocks.md: **Silver**, **copper**, **aluminium** and **steel**.

front_blocks.md: Name four examples of **insulators**.

back_blocks.md: **Rubber**, **plastic**, **glass** and **wood**.

front_blocks.md: On an atomic scale, why do metals conduct electricity so well?

back_blocks.md: Metals consist of positively charged metal ions with their outermost electrons **delocalised** (free to move). Since current is the rate of flow of electrons, the more easily electrons can move, the better the conductor.

back_blocks.md: In a conductor, the outermost electrons of the metal ions are **delocalised**, meaning they are free to move.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Insulators such as wood never conduct any charge at all.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Some non-metals, such as **wood**, allow a little charge to pass through them in the form of **static** electricity, even though they are not good conductors.

front_blocks.md: What is the aim of the core practical investigating charging by friction?

back_blocks.md: To investigate how insulating materials can be charged by friction.

front_blocks.md: Define **static electricity**.

back_blocks.md: **Static electricity** is the accumulation of **charge** on an object, which can then attract other objects or produce sparks.

cards.front_md: Define **static electricity**.
cards.back_md: **Static electricity** is the accumulation of **charge** on an object, which can then attract other objects or produce sparks.

front_blocks.md: Define **non-contact force**.

back_blocks.md: A **non-contact force** is a force that acts on an object without the objects being physically in contact with each other, such as the electric force between two charged objects.

cards.front_md: Define **non-contact force**.
cards.back_md: A **non-contact force** is a force that acts on an object without the objects being physically in contact with each other, such as the electric force between two charged objects.

front_blocks.md: What determines whether two charged objects attract or repel each other?

back_blocks.md: **Like** charges (both positive or both negative) **repel**; **opposite** charges (one positive, one negative) **attract**.

cards.front_md: What determines whether two charged objects attract or repel each other?
cards.back_md: **Like** charges (both positive or both negative) **repel**; **opposite** charges (one positive, one negative) **attract**.

front_blocks.md: How does the distance between two charged objects affect the electric force between them?

back_blocks.md: The force is **stronger** when the objects are **closer together**.

cards.front_md: How does the distance between two charged objects affect the electric force between them?
cards.back_md: The force is **stronger** when the objects are **closer together**.

front_blocks.md: Why is the overall charge of a neutral atom zero?

back_blocks.md: A neutral atom contains an equal number of protons (positive) and electrons (negative), so the equal but opposite charges cancel out.

cards.front_md: Why is the overall charge of a neutral atom zero?

front_blocks.md: Charging by friction occurs when negatively charged **______** are transferred from one insulating material to another.

back_blocks.md: Charging by friction occurs when negatively charged **electrons** are transferred from one insulating material to another.

front_blocks.md: In charging by friction, which object becomes negatively charged and which becomes positively charged?

back_blocks.md: The object that electrons transfer **to** becomes **negatively** charged. The object that electrons transfer **from** becomes **positively** charged.

cards.front_md: In charging by friction, which object becomes negatively charged and which becomes positively charged?
cards.back_md: The object that electrons transfer **to** becomes **negatively** charged. The object that electrons transfer **from** becomes **positively** charged.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
When charging by friction, positive charge moves from one insulator to the other.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Only **electrons** (negative charge) move during charging by friction; an object that loses electrons is left with an equal **positive** charge.

front_blocks.md: How does a photocopier use static electricity to copy a document?

back_blocks.md: An image is projected onto a positively charged copying plate, which loses charge in light areas but keeps positive charge in dark (text) areas. Negatively charged toner powder sticks to the positively charged areas and is transferred to paper, which is heated to fix the toner.

front_blocks.md: Why is insecticide given an electrostatic charge as it leaves a sprayer?

back_blocks.md: The charged droplets **repel** each other (same charge), keeping the spray fine and spread over a large area. They are also **attracted** to the Earth's opposite charge, so they fall quickly and are less likely to blow away.

front_blocks.md: Define **earthing**.

back_blocks.md: **Earthing** is connecting an object (e.g. a vehicle) to the Earth using a conductor, allowing a build-up of charge to flow away safely instead of causing a spark.

front_blocks.md: Why is a build-up of static charge dangerous when refuelling an aeroplane?

back_blocks.md: Friction between the flammable fuel (an insulator) and the pipe causes the fuel to **gain charge**. If this charge produced a spark, the fuel could ignite and cause an explosion.

cards.front_md: Why is a build-up of static charge dangerous when refuelling an aeroplane?
cards.back_md: Friction between the flammable fuel (an insulator) and the pipe causes the fuel to **gain charge**. If this charge produced a spark, the fuel could ignite and cause an explosion.

front_blocks.md: How does the bonding line reduce the risk of sparking when refuelling an aeroplane?

back_blocks.md: The **bonding line** is a copper wire connecting the fuel tank to the Earth. It is easier for charge to flow down the bonding line than to spark, so it carries the charge away and removes the risk of sparks.

front_blocks.md: Define a **spark**, in the context of static hazards.

back_blocks.md: A **spark** is current travelling through the air between two objects, caused when a large build-up of charge produces a potential difference across a gap that is large enough to break down the air.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Static electricity is only ever dangerous, with no everyday practical uses.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Static electricity is put to practical use in **photocopiers**, **inkjet printers** and **insecticide sprayers**, as well as posing dangers such as sparking.
